why_how.text: Newer-vehicle assistance features save lives and curb injuries when properly used.
Some features only warn, while others take over braking or steering.

scenario.text: Eva's car beeps and vibrates as she drifts toward another lane.

reasoning.text: A warning system alerts through sound or vibration, while an assist system would seize braking or steering.

result.text: Eva recognizes a warning, not an assist, and steers back herself.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking assistance features work equally well in any weather.

correction.text: Rain, snow, ice, fog, grades and bends can defeat features, so drivers stay skeptical in those conditions.

memory_support.text: Warnings notice; assists intervene; you still drive.

prompt.text: Your car alerts you with a sound but does not brake. What kind of system is that?

rationale.text: Warning systems only alert through sound or vibration, while assist systems seize braking or steering.

narration.text: This chapter covers the driver assistance features found on many newer vehicles. The manual says they save lives and curb injuries when they are properly used. In this first lesson we look at how they work, which features are common, and the key difference between features that only warn you and features that take over braking or steering. Then we turn to what the features ask of you: steady focus, knowing your owner's manual and the features' limits, and keeping the sensors and software in good shape. The next lessons cover how these features are treated on the road test.

lines.text: Alert, or take over braking or steering.

narration.text: Assistance features work by sensing and watching conditions around the vehicle, spotting dangers that are present or coming, and helping you avoid a crash. They do that in one of two ways. Some give an alert, such as a sound or a vibration. Others take over braking or steering. The manual stresses that they save lives and curb injuries when properly used. So the features are a second set of senses for the car, and some of them can act on what they sense, but the benefit depends on how the driver uses them.

The manual lists common assistance features. They include blind-spot warning, back-up cameras, forward-collision warning, automatic emergency braking, lane-keeping assistance and active parking assist, among others. Some of these only warn, like blind-spot warning and forward-collision warning. Others act, like automatic emergency braking, which brakes for you, and lane-keeping assistance, which steers. Back-up cameras help you see behind the car. Knowing which group a feature belongs to tells you what to expect from it, and whether it will only alert you or will actually take some control of the vehicle.

lines.text: Some features adjust braking or steering.
Stay focused and check mirrors always.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Drivers sometimes assume every feature will act to save them. ADAS safety features may provide alerts such as sounds or vibrations, or they may take control by adjusting braking or steering. So if your car beeps when you drift, that is a warning, and you must do the steering. If your car brakes on its own, that is an assist. Knowing which kind you have tells you whether the next move is yours or the car's, and with a warning it is always yours.

lines.text: Know the owner's manual and limits.
Be skeptical in bad weather, hills, curves.

narration.text: Driving a vehicle with assistance features demands constant focus. Learn your owner's manual so you know how each feature works, and learn the features' limits. Stay skeptical in rain, snow, ice and fog, and on grades and bends, because those conditions can defeat the features. So the features do not reduce what you need to pay attention to. If anything, you must know when they may not work. A feature that performs well on a clear, straight road may fail on a snowy curve, and the driver has to be ready for that.

Keep the sensors clean and undamaged, and keep the software current according to the maker's guidance where that applies. The manual ties proper use directly to results: used properly, these features promise fewer crashes, injuries and deaths. So caring for the system is part of using it properly. Clean, whole sensors and current software are the two care steps the manual names. Treat sensor care like any other routine check on your vehicle, so the features are ready when you need them.

Here is a quick check: your car makes a warning sound as you close in on the car ahead, but it does not brake. Who must apply the brakes? Work it out before reading on. You must brake immediately, because some features provide sound or vibration alerts while others adjust braking or steering, and you remain responsible at all times. So in that moment, the braking is up to you. Remember too that rain, snow, ice, fog, grades and bends can defeat features, and that keeping sensors clean and software current is part of using them properly.

To close, assistance features save lives and curb injuries when properly used, by sensing conditions, spotting dangers and helping you avoid crashes through alerts or by taking over braking or steering. Common features include blind-spot warning, back-up cameras, forward-collision warning, automatic emergency braking, lane keeping and active parking assist. Features may alert you or adjust braking or steering. Driving with them demands constant focus, knowledge of the manual and limits, and skepticism in bad weather, on hills and on curves. Keep sensors clean and software current. Next we look at the road test.

why_how.text: Road tests forbid parking assist and cruise control because features assist rather than drive.

scenario.text: Sam plans to use adaptive cruise control on the highway part of his road test.

reasoning.text: Testing bans adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking, the lone prohibitions.

result.text: Sam keeps adaptive cruise control off and controls his own speed.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that using only permitted features guarantees a pass on the driving part.

correction.text: Allowed features still fail candidates who lean on them, since examiners score unassisted safe operation.

memory_support.text: The features assist; you drive; the examiner decides.

prompt.text: Which two features are banned during the road test?

answer.text: Adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking.

rationale.text: These are the lone prohibitions; other listed features are permitted but must not be leaned on.

narration.text: This lesson is about how driver assistance features are treated on the road test. The manual explains why road tests forbid parking assist and cruise control, names the two features that are banned outright during testing, and explains how the examiner scores your driving. The key idea is that the features assist, but you drive. The next lesson lists the many features that are permitted, but even those come with a warning: leaning on them can still cost you. So we start here with the doctrine behind the rules, then the bans, then scoring.

lines.text: Road tests forbid parking assist, cruise control.
Head checks, mirrors and cameras stay yours.

narration.text: Road tests forbid parking assist and cruise control. The reason the manual gives is that features assist rather than drive. That leaves you engaged and focused, doing your own head checks and using mirrors and cameras, while you own safe operation of the vehicle. You never lean on the gadgets alone. The manual sums it up: assistance never replaces engaged driving with checks, mirrors and cameras. So on the test, the examiner wants to see you driving, not the car. The features may be there, but the responsibility is entirely yours.

Testing bans exactly two features: adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking. The manual calls these the lone prohibitions. Every other feature on its testing list is permitted. So before the test, make sure adaptive cruise control is not in use and that you will park without automatic parallel parking. You will control your own speed and do your own parking maneuver. Keep the two banned features in mind, because they are the ones a question is most likely to ask about, and because they connect directly to the doctrine that features assist rather than drive.

lines.text: Permitted features can still fail you.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Candidates sometimes think that if a feature is permitted, they can rely on it. The manual says allowed features still fail candidates who lean on them, since examiners score unassisted safe operation, and their scoring is final. So a permitted blind-spot monitor does not replace your own head check. A back-up camera does not replace looking behind you. The examiner is judging whether you can drive safely without depending on the features, and the examiner's decision is the one that counts.

Here is a quick check: which two features are banned during the road test? Work it out before reading on. The answer is adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking, the lone prohibitions. Other listed features are permitted during testing. But remember the catch: even permitted features can fail a candidate who leans on them, because examiners score unassisted safe operation and have the final say. If you were thinking of blind-spot monitoring or back-up cameras, those are permitted, as long as you still do your own checks.

To wrap up, road tests forbid parking assist and cruise control, since features assist rather than drive, leaving you engaged and focused with head checks, mirrors and cameras while you own safe operation. Assistance never replaces engaged driving. Testing bans adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking, the lone prohibitions. Examiners judge unassisted safe operation and reliance-free driving, with final scoring authority, so permitted features can still fail a candidate who leans on them. Next we list the features that are permitted during testing.

why_how.text: Many warning systems and some assists are permitted during testing.
Sensing features stay permitted while the two steering-or-speed features stay banned.

scenario.text: Kai's test car has parking sensors and automatic parallel parking.

reasoning.text: Parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts stay permitted while automatic parallel parking itself stays banned.

result.text: Kai keeps the parking sensors on but parks the car himself.

claim.text: Common mistake: thinking that because automatic parallel parking is banned, all parking aids are banned.

correction.text: Parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts stay permitted; only automatic parallel parking is banned, sensing versus steering.

memory_support.text: Sense, warn and brake are fine; cruise and self-park are not.

prompt.text: During the road test, may you use automatic emergency braking?

rationale.text: Emergency braking, reverse braking, lane keeping and left-turn avoidance test freely, while adaptive cruise and automatic parallel parking never do.

narration.text: This lesson lists the assistance features that are permitted during testing. The manual groups them: warnings and cameras, detection and alert systems, parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts, and a set of braking and steering assists. We will go through each group and then contrast the permitted features with the two that are banned, which we covered in the last lesson. The contrast has a pattern that makes it easier to remember. Keep the last lesson's warning in mind too: permitted does not mean you may rely on a feature instead of driving.

The first group of permitted features covers warnings and cameras. Testing permits back-up warning, blind-spot monitoring and warning, and rear sideview and surround-view cameras. These help you see and notice what is around the car. They do not take control. So during the test, a blind-spot warning may light up or a camera may show the view behind you, and that is allowed. You still do your own head checks and mirror checks, because the examiner scores your safe operation, not the feature's. These features add information, and you act on it.

The next group is detection and alert systems. Testing further permits curve-speed warning, detection of bicycles, pedestrians and obstacles, forward-collision warning, high-speed alert, and lane-departure warning. Then, to complete the warning systems, parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts are also permitted. All of these alert you to something, a curve taken too fast, a person or object ahead, a car closing in, or a drift out of your lane. Like the cameras, they give you notice. They do not drive for you, which is why the manual allows them during testing.

Some assists that actually act are also permitted. Testing permits automatic emergency braking and brake assist, automatic reverse braking, lane-keeping assist, and left-turn crash avoidance. These can brake or steer to help avoid a crash. They are allowed during testing, but the same rule applies as for every feature: you must not lean on them. The examiner still judges whether you drive safely on your own. So you may leave these systems on, but you should drive as though they were not there, braking and steering yourself as the situation requires.

lines.text: Four assists yes, two features no.

narration.text: Here is the trap. Because automatic parallel parking is banned, people assume all parking help is banned. The manual draws the line between sensing and steering. Parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts stay permitted, while automatic parallel parking itself stays banned. A broader pattern holds too: emergency braking, reverse braking, lane keeping and left-turn avoidance test freely, yet adaptive cruise and automatic parallel parking test never, four yeses against two noes. So sensing and crash-avoiding assists are in, while the two features that take over speed or the parking maneuver are out.

Here is a quick check: during the road test, may you use automatic emergency braking? Work it out before reading on. The answer is yes, it is permitted, along with brake assist, automatic reverse braking, lane-keeping assist and left-turn crash avoidance. The two features that are never permitted are adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking. If you were unsure because emergency braking takes over braking, remember the pattern: these four assists test freely, and only those two features are banned. Even so, you must not lean on the permitted ones.

To close, testing permits back-up warning, blind-spot monitoring and warning, rear sideview and surround-view cameras, curve-speed warning, bicycle, pedestrian and obstacle detection, forward-collision warning, high-speed alert, lane-departure warning, parking sensors and rear cross-traffic alerts. It also permits automatic emergency braking and brake assist, automatic reverse braking, lane-keeping assist and left-turn crash avoidance. Only adaptive cruise control and automatic parallel parking are banned. Sensing is in, self-parking is out. That completes the chapter on driver assistance features.
